questions.prompt: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated which pair of study techniques high utility?
options: Practice testing and distributed practice
Rereading and highlighting the chapter text
Summarizing and keyword mnemonics
Imagery use and rereading together

questions.prompt: Dunlosky et al. graded 10 techniques and rated 2 of them high utility. What percent of the techniques earned the top rating?
Put the steps of an evidence-based study session in order.
steps: Read the section once
Close the book and recall the key points
Check your recall against the text
Schedule the next review a few days out

questions.prompt: Find the faulty step in this study plan.
steps: Read the chapter once
Highlight the key sentences
Reread the highlights three times as the main review
Take a self-quiz the next day
questions.fix: Rereading highlights is low utility; replace it with retrieval practice.

questions.prompt: Match each technique to its Dunlosky utility rating.
Flavell (1979) split metacognition into which two parts?
options: Knowledge and regulation
Memory and attention span
Reading and writing skills
Speed and accuracy of recall

questions.prompt: You predicted you would get 9 of 10 quiz items right and got 6. By how many percentage points did you overestimate?
Order the metacognitive regulation cycle.
steps: Plan how to approach the task
Monitor your understanding while working
Evaluate the result against the goal
Adjust your strategy for next time

questions.prompt: Find the step that breaks self-monitoring.
steps: Set a goal for the session
Attempt practice problems without notes
Judge mastery by how familiar the page looks
Compare answers with the key
questions.fix: Judge mastery from recall performance; familiarity is a poor signal.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.meaning: What you know about how you learn
Tracking how well you understand right now
Changing strategy in response to what you notice

questions.prompt: Why does rereading feel effective?
options: Familiarity is mistaken for mastery
It produces the strongest long-term memory
It forces retrieval
It spaces practice automatically

questions.prompt: In Kornell and Bjork's study 90% learned better from spacing and 72% believed massing was better. What is the gap between those two figures in percentage points?
Order the steps to test whether a feeling of knowing is real.
steps: Notice the page feels familiar
Cover the page
Try to state the idea from memory
Compare your answer with the source

questions.prompt: Find the flawed inference.
steps: I reread the chapter twice
The second read felt smooth
So I have learned the material
I will check with a closed-book quiz
questions.fix: Smooth rereading shows familiarity; only a recall test shows learning.

questions.prompt: Match each experience to what it signals.
Which activity is retrieval practice?
options: Writing what you remember with the book closed
Rereading your notes the night before
Highlighting the summary in yellow ink
Copying the textbook definition word for word

questions.prompt: A deck has 40 cards. A learner recalls 28 on the first self-test. What percent did they retrieve?
Order the steps of one retrieval round.
steps: Read the prompt
Recall the answer without looking
Reveal the correct answer
Rate how hard the recall was

questions.prompt: Find the step that turns this into restudy.
steps: Show the question
Show the answer beside the question
Ask the learner to say the answer
Record whether they were right
questions.fix: Hide the answer until after the learner attempts recall.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.meaning: Recall strengthens memory more than re-exposure
Showing the correct answer after an attempt

questions.prompt: Which schedule uses spacing for a test in two weeks?
options: Four short sessions spread over two weeks
One four-hour session the night before
Two sessions back to back on one evening
Rereading notes daily without any testing

questions.prompt: A review schedule doubles the gap each time: 1, 2, 4, 8 days. How many days after the first study is the fifth review if the first review is 1 day after study?
Order a spaced schedule for one card.
steps: Learn the card
Review it the next day
Review it about a week later
Review it about a month later

questions.prompt: Find the step that undoes the spacing.
steps: Study the topic on Monday
Review it on Wednesday
Review it twice more on Wednesday night
Review it the following Monday
questions.fix: Back-to-back repeats in one night are massed; spread them across days.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.meaning: Time between last study and the test

questions.prompt: What makes this the textbook case of a wrong belief?
options: Most learners did better with spacing yet believed massing was better
Learners did better with massing than with spacing
Most learners had no opinion about either schedule
Spacing and massing gave identical results in every test

questions.prompt: In a class of 50, 90% learn better with spacing. How many students is that?
Order the Kornell and Bjork style experiment.
steps: Learners study some items massed and some spaced
Learners take a test on all items
Researchers compare scores by condition
Learners report which method they think worked better

questions.prompt: Find the error in this conclusion.
steps: 90% scored higher with spacing
72% said massing worked better
So learners' beliefs track their results
Beliefs about learning need outside checks
questions.fix: The beliefs were inverted relative to results; they did not track them.

questions.prompt: Match each figure to what it measured.

pairs.meaning: Learners who did better with spacing
Learners who believed massing was better

questions.prompt: Which is a desirable difficulty?
options: Interleaving problem types
Rereading a summary until it feels easy
Using a larger font
Studying in silence

questions.prompt: Group A scores 80% right after blocked practice and 50% a week later. Group B scores 65% then 60%. How many percentage points more does B retain at one week?
Order how a desirable difficulty pays off.
steps: Practice feels harder
Performance during practice dips
Effortful retrieval strengthens memory
Long-term retention rises

questions.prompt: Find the faulty reasoning.
steps: The quiz session felt slow and hard
My practice scores were lower than with rereading
So the quiz session was a waste
I will check retention next week
questions.fix: Lower in-session performance is expected; judge by delayed retention.

questions.prompt: Match each technique to the difficulty it adds.

pairs.meaning: Choosing the method for each problem

questions.prompt: Interleaving helps most with which skill?
options: Telling problem types apart and choosing a method
Typing speed on a standard keyboard layout every day
Recognizing a page you have already read twice
Memorizing one formula word for word

questions.prompt: A set has 3 problem types with 4 problems each, fully interleaved so no two adjacent problems share a type. How many type switches occur across the 12 problems?
Order the steps for an interleaved session.
steps: Pick several related problem types
Shuffle the problems together
Identify the type before solving each one
Check which identifications were wrong

questions.prompt: Find the step that turns this into blocking.
steps: Collect area problems for three shapes
Sort them so all circles come first, then triangles, then squares
Solve each problem
Check answers
questions.fix: Mix the shapes so each problem needs a fresh choice of formula.

questions.prompt: Match each schedule to its pattern.
Which prompt is elaborative interrogation?
options: Why is this fact true?
What page is this on?
How many words is the definition?
What color was the heading?

questions.prompt: A learner writes a why-explanation for 12 of 20 facts. What fraction, as a percent, got an explanation?
Order a self-explanation step on a worked example.
steps: Read one line of the worked example
Ask what that line does and why
Connect it to something you already know
Say the explanation in your own words

questions.prompt: Find the step that is not self-explanation.
steps: Read the step in the solution
Ask why this step follows
Copy the step word for word into notes
Link the step to a rule you know
questions.fix: Copying adds no meaning; explain the step in your own words.

questions.prompt: Match each technique to its definition.

pairs.meaning: Explaining why a stated fact is true
Relating new information to what you know

questions.prompt: What did Pashler et al. (2008) find about the meshing hypothesis?
options: Almost no evidence supports it
Strong evidence supports it
It works only for visual learners
It works only for children

questions.prompt: To test meshing, learners of 2 styles get each of 2 teaching modes. How many style-by-mode groups does the full crossover design need?
Order the crossover test for learning styles.
steps: Classify learners by preferred style
Randomly assign each to matched or mismatched teaching
Test everyone on the same material
Check whether matched beats mismatched for every style

questions.prompt: Find the unsupported step.
steps: Survey students on preferred style
Label each student visual, auditory or kinesthetic
Teach each student only in their style to raise scores
Measure outcomes with a common test
questions.fix: Matching instruction to style has no evidence of raising scores; match the method to the content.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.meaning: A preferred mode of taking in information
Teaching in the preferred mode improves learning
The pattern needed to support meshing
